headline: UK's Immigrant Students Outperform Peers—And Nobody Knows Why
meta_description: First- and second-generation immigrant children in the UK score higher than peers on international tests, puzzling education experts across the OECD.
summary_short: A rare bright spot: UK immigrant students average 1.2 points higher on OECD math, science and reading tests than non-immigrant peers.
body:
First- and second-generation immigrant students in the UK score, on average, 1.2 points higher than non-immigrant students across the OECD's math, science and reading tests. The achievement places Britain among a small group of countries—including Cyprus and Montenegro—where children from immigrant families consistently outperform their peers.

The pattern stands out in global education rankings as genuinely unusual. Most nations struggle to close achievement gaps between immigrant and native-born students, making the UK's consistent success a genuine anomaly.

But here's the puzzle: policymakers have no clear explanation for why this is happening. The gap isn't trivial, and it's consistent across multiple subjects and testing frameworks. Understanding the mechanisms behind Britain's success could offer valuable lessons for education systems worldwide facing similar demographic shifts.
quick_facts: UK immigrant students score 1.2 points higher on OECD tests
Includes first- and second-generation immigrant children
Tests cover math, science, and reading across OECD nations
UK joins Cyprus and Montenegro as rare success cases
